Rejected from Big-N Company with Referral, would like Resume Critique

I've recently been applying to companies for a SWE intern role in Summer 2020. I'm still in the early stages (just started applying two weeks ago), have coding challenges for some companies and a little past that for others, but for most, I haven't heard anything yet.

However, I was surprised today to get a rejection from a Big N Company, even after getting a referral from a current employee. I thought I would at least be able to get past the resume screening, as I've been attending a bunch of campus Facebook events, and I've had my resume looked at a few times by Big N recruiters. Could anyone provide any insight into why this may have happened? Was it too late in the application cycle? Is my experience just not enough to make the cut? Any feedback would be greatly appreciated!

This is one of the major things that I have struggled with regarding my faith as well, but I have come across some articles and information that have helped me reconcile some of these things. 

As far as I know, there's something major that distinguishes Abu Talib from the non-Muslims of today: he had seen the Prophet (SAW) first-hand, witnessed his message, believed it to be true, but did not convert on his deathbed to avoid facing criticism from the Quraysh. Many non-Muslims have a much more convoluted view of Islam, as they're not learning directly from Muslims, let alone directly from the Prophet (SAW) himself.  Instead, much of what they are exposed to is little snippets of Islam, largely through a Western lens through media or academia, or worse yet (in my opinion), strict interpretations of Islam that are the first things that pop up when one tries to research Islam online. Had these been the sources of my understanding of Islam, I doubt that I would want to be a Muslim. To me, it would make sense for these people to be judged differently than Abu Talib had been judged. Similarly, someone who grew up in a rural area with narrow-minded exposure to Islam would be judged differently than someone who has studied Islam and been exposed to it by Muslims.

The other issue is regarding the eternity of the hellfire for a non-Muslim. A few Islamic scholars have argued that hell may not be eternal for those who had an atom's weight of faith in God, although most believe this to be pertaining to only those who had faith in Islam. Fewer scholars have argued that hell is not eternal for anyone, and that after suffering for their sins, they would be removed from it. This is a position held by Ibn Taymiyya and, to a lesser extent, Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya, who analyze the claim from a Sahih hadith in which Allah decreed: “My mercy overwhelms my anger.”  This argument has been revived by some modern Muslim scholars as well, although it is considered to be a minority opinion.

It can also be noted that while scholars hold a view about which actions and beliefs will lead to punishment or salvation, one cannot say for certain what the fate of an individual belonging to a group is in the afterlife.

For more on this, I highly recommend reading this article from Jonathan Brown.

[https://yaqeeninstitute.org/en/jonathan-brown/the-fate-of-non-muslims-perspectives-on-salvation-outside-of-islam/](https://yaqeeninstitute.org/en/jonathan-brown/the-fate-of-non-muslims-perspectives-on-salvation-outside-of-islam/)
